Who this handout is for

This handout supports students studying induction, generators and transformers in AQA GCSE Physics Higher. It is the AQA Higher resource, separate from the Edexcel induction handout in the resource library.

Thirteen teaching sections combine diagrams, core concepts, exam tips, worked calculations and numbered exercise sets with subquestions. Four pages of solutions provide classroom marking points for all 13 sets.

17 pages · 13 exercise sets · Solutions with marking points

What the handout covers

  • The generator effect and factors affecting induced potential difference
  • Lenz's law and forces opposing the change
  • Alternators, slip rings and output graphs
  • Split-ring dynamos and pulsating direct current
  • Bicycle generators, peak p.d. and frequency
  • Moving-coil microphones and energy transfer
  • Transformer operation and voltage/turns ratios
  • Ideal-transformer power and current calculations
  • High-voltage transmission and the National Grid

A focused topic handout, not a complete GCSE Physics revision guide. Independent Study with Dr teaching material, not an official AQA publication or official examination mark scheme. Existing figure credits are retained in the PDF.

Key ideas at a glance

Distinguish induced p.d. from induced current

A conductor cutting magnetic field lines, or a changing magnetic field linking a coil, induces a potential difference. Current additionally requires a complete conducting circuit. A stationary magnet inside a stationary coil produces no sustained induced p.d.

Use the change to explain direction

In a complete circuit, the induced current produces a magnetic field opposing the change that caused it. A north pole approaching a coil makes its near end north; withdrawing that pole makes the near end south.

Read generator graphs carefully

An alternator produces alternating polarity; a simple split-ring dynamo produces one polarity but a varying magnitude. A bicycle generator with a rotating magnet can produce a.c. Faster rotation increases frequency as well as peak p.d.; more turns alone do not change frequency at fixed rotation speed.

Keep transformer quantities on the correct side

Use Vs/Vp = Ns/Np for the turns ratio and VpIp = VsIs for an ideal transformer. Raising voltage does not increase power: at the same transferred power it reduces current, reducing cable heating during transmission.
